Materials and spoken prompts for these examples

Adult: draw and supply the actual empty-pot, planting and green-shoot pictures before any picture-sequence task. For topic/detail prompts, draw a sprouted bean with its white root and two leaves. For the caterpillar check, say: “I found a caterpillar. It was green and had tiny legs.” Read this original mini-text for the Niko response: “Niko could not find his boot. He looked under the bench. There it was! He put it on and could go home.” A response may name relief and link it to finding the boot. The pictures and text must be supplied; labels alone are not picture evidence.

Speak about an event

Adult supplies: “We filled a pot, planted a seed and watered it.” The learner chooses the opening and two ordered details, then tells the report to a real listener. A clear topic, relevant order and comfortable actual volume are the response criteria.

Complete check prompts and response guidance

Complete the checks with these supplied alternatives. Caterpillar topic: “its green body and tiny legs” / “my lunch”. Opening: “I found a caterpillar” / “I forgot my shoes”. Class volume: “comfortably audible” / “a whisper nobody hears” / “a shout beside someone’s ear”. Event order: “found it, looked closely, told the class” / “told the class, then found it yesterday”. The first option in each pair or set fits the given purpose. For open personal reports, accept accurate relevant alternatives and observe real delivery.

Materials and spoken prompts for these examples

Adult: supply the school-approved upper-case and lower-case models, writing guides, starts and stroke directions before each handwriting task. Demonstrate each selected letter live. The on-screen case samples identify letters; they are not stroke-order diagrams. Family groupings depend on the taught script and are prompts for comparison, not a universal movement rule. Use the full alphabet over several short sessions, not a compulsory single sitting.

Full case identification samples

A a · B b · C c · D d · E e · F f · G g · H h · I i · J j · K k · L l · M m · N n · O o · P p · Q q · R r · S s · T t · U u · V v · W w · X x · Y y · Z z. These are screen-font identification samples. Obtain the corresponding school writing models before practising formation.

Complete check prompts and response guidance

Complete the checks with these alternatives. Before writing, look at “the taught start and movement” / “only the colour of the pencil”. The start matters because “it supports the taught movement” / “it makes every letter begin in the same place”. Same-letter case pair: A–a / A–b. Correct partner: M–m / M–n. The first option answers each check. These recognition questions do not replace observing formation.

Materials and spoken prompts for these examples

Adult: speak every word before the child responds; hide adult print where reading would change the listening task. For picture/object tasks, prepare actual pictures or safe objects for cake, lake, fish; sun and sock; moon and map; and a rabbit. Name each aloud. Draw the lake as water and cake as food so labels are not the only cues. Invite another valid spoken rhyme and use the child’s natural pronunciation.

Fresh oral sound check

Adult says dog. Ask for its syllable count and final phoneme. It has one syllable and ends in /g/. Ask for a new rhyme and a phrase beginning like dog; log and dancing dog are possible responses. Accept locally valid alternatives.

Complete check prompts and response guidance

Adult: say each set aloud. Rhyming pair: cake–lake / cake–fish. Rhyme for cat: hat / dog. Alliteration: helpful Henry / helpful Mia. Repeated /b/ beginning: busy bee / happy bee. The first choice fits each stated pattern. Also ask the child for a new rhyme for hen, an alliterative pair beginning like moon, the beats in rabbit, and the first sound of sun. Possible answers: pen; moon/map; two; /s/.

Materials and spoken prompts for these examples

Adult: deliver actual speech. For picture choices, prepare and name drawings of mat and sat (a person sitting), sun and run (a person running), and map and mop; demonstrate meanings before the listening choice. Use safe counters and change only the specified sound position. Sound notation is for the adult: short i in lip is /ɪ/, not the long ee sound. No picture or written response certifies heard sound without a real oral turn.

Three oral operations, exact positions

Adult says tea, adds /m/ at the end and waits for team; says best, removes internal /s/ and waits for bet; says mop, replaces first /m/ with /t/ and waits for top. Use one operation at a time. New letters are not shown and spelling changes are not assessed.

Complete check prompts and response guidance

Adult: say each target aloud. I | can | hop has three words; The | dog | ran has three words. Can has /k/ /æ/ /n/. Blend /l/ /ɪ/ /p/ to make lip. In additional fresh checks say “at” plus initial /m/ (mat), “smile” minus initial /s/ (mile), and “pin” with its middle changed to the vowel in pen (pen). Ask the child to say which sounds changed and which stayed.

Materials and spoken prompts for these examples

Adult: prepare the learner’s preferred printed name plus two real distractor name cards, checking the correct spelling with the learner. Supply the actual case cards named in each task. If using cue pictures, draw and name the selected objects from the alphabet reference; the child may instead hear the word spoken. Ask name and sound as separate questions. Print or select small sets across sessions and revisit all 26 letters in both cases.

Check the exceptional cues

Final x in fox represents /k/ + /s/, two phonemes. In queen, show the team qu for /k/ + /w/. The letter q is named cue; do not call the whole team one sound belonging to isolated q. Y/y is named why; its beginning sound in yes differs from its name.

Complete check prompts and response guidance

Actual printed check choices: A’s lower-case partner is a, not b; m’s upper-case partner is M, not N. For m’s common sound choose the humming beginning of moon rather than its letter name em. For s choose the hissing beginning of sun rather than its name ess. These four checks sample only two letters; use the full reference to revisit both cases and separate names from sounds across all 26.

Materials and spoken prompts for these examples

Adult: supply real dictated speech for spelling, hiding the answer until the attempt. For any picture task, prepare and name a sun drawing, and simple cat, dog and map drawings before the activity. The learner reads by blending the printed word, then checks the picture’s meaning. For the sun try, say “sun” without revealing its spelling. CVC work here uses previously taught simple one-letter correspondences.

A fresh middle-sound comparison

Printed words: hen / hot. Adult reads both after the learner tries. E in hen and o in hot are different middle-vowel spellings; the final consonants also differ, so this is not a one-position substitution. For a one-position change use hen → pen, changing only the initial h to p.

Complete check prompts and response guidance

Adult: say cat and dog without displaying their spellings for the writing checks. Cat uses c-a-t; dog uses d-o-g. For the separate reading checks show c-a-t and m-a-p; the learner blends cat and map. Printed spelling choices, if using recognition support: cat / cta and dog / dgo. Selecting a spelling is supported recognition, not independent writing from dictation.

Materials and spoken prompts for these examples

Adult: say the intended whole word without showing its spelling before every independent spelling turn. For picture tasks, prepare and name simple map, fish, dog and several-dogs drawings. For ending-card support supply dog, s and t: dogs matches more than one dog; dogt does not. Distinguish a plausible sound-based attempt from conventional spelling and record which letters and teams were already taught.

First, middle and final repair

Adult says bag. Compare written bg, ag and ba only after an independent attempt. Bg misses the vowel a; ag misses initial b; ba misses final g. Rebuild bag and read back the whole word after each repair.

Complete check prompts and response guidance

Supply the choices omitted from the quick prompts: map / mp / pam for map; sun / sn / nus for sun; fish / fih / fsh for fish. The first spelling in each set completely represents the intended taught sound sequence. When unsure, first say and segment the whole word, rather than guess its first letter. For independent spelling, dictate a fresh word without displaying these choices or its answer.

Materials and spoken prompts for these examples

Adult: supply the exact preferred name or familiar label model and any photo/name cards before using a personal example. Confirm its spelling and pronunciation with the learner. For a shared-text word hunt, use this complete original text: “My dog is on the rug. My cat is on the mat. The dog can sit.” Find my/My twice, is twice and the/The as printed. Discuss capitals at sentence beginnings. Teach known sound links and any unusual parts of the target words.

A complete sentence choice

Use the exact alternatives is / and / my in “The dog ____ here.” Is completes this supplied sentence. Context supports meaning, but inspect i-s rather than guess. For the repair example, show “Teh dog si on the rug” and compare t-h-e and i-s with the intended complete sentence.

Complete check prompts and response guidance

Use four different taught targets for the four repeated common-word prompts: (1) and / ant; (2) my / mud; (3) is / ink; (4) the / ten. An adult reads the named target and the child selects it, then reads or communicates the chosen word. The first option matches each target. All alternatives are real words: frequency is not a property a child can infer from an unexplained list. Follow with genuine reading and covered-model writing of some taught words.

Materials and spoken prompts for these examples

Adult: prepare an actual drawing of one dog and another of three dogs, plus dog and dogs cards, before the dog-picture tasks. Supply one cup and three cups for the cup tasks. Draw and name a sun and a hat before joining sunhat; show or draw a raincoat for raincoat. The picture meaning must be available, not merely a written label. Read all words aloud if needed; the goal is meaning parts, not independent decoding.

Meaning family or just rhyme?

Compare cat, cats and hat. Cat and cats share the base meaning cat; s adds more than one. Cat and hat rhyme, but hat is not built from the base cat. Compare bus and buses only orally if useful; do not claim the final s of bus is itself a plural ending.

Complete check prompts and response guidance

Complete the quick checks: dog names an animal rather than a colour; s in dogs shows more than one; dogs has two meaningful parts in this example, dog and s; cats means more than one cat. Compare cat / cats as actual printed alternatives. Read these aloud if decoding would hide the intended meaning skill.
